Answer2: Legacy Salesforce Visualforce/Apex and Mule 3 applications are costly to modernize because developers must reconstruct dependencies, preserve behavior and security, translate platform-specific syntax, and prove that generated changes are safe. This project supports developers, DevOps engineers, and technical leads responsible for application modernization. It provides a conversational, evidence-backed workflow that turns a bounded legacy component into a reviewable migration candidate while keeping source selection, scope, validation, and external actions under deterministic and human control.
Answer3: The goal is to demonstrate that an LLM-based agent can migrate a bounded, dependency-closed legacy unit into an additive, locally validated candidate. The implemented scope includes two synthetic Salesforce Visualforce/Apex-to-LWC/Apex units—Account/Contact and a nontrivial Case Management console—and one Mule 3-to-Mule 4 customer-status API. Candidates include implementation, metadata, and tests. The prototype does not accept an arbitrary repository, perform bulk migration, replace legacy components destructively, deploy to Salesforce or Anypoint, commit code, or claim production readiness.
Answer4: The system has exactly three LLM roles: Architect, Engineer, and Validator. A deterministic Python/LangGraph controller—not a fourth agent—owns paths, policies, human gates, tools, retries, state, and disposition. Before the Architect, it builds a strict GraphAssuranceReport from the frozen source and dependency graph. Only an assured, digest-bound report permits planning; review_required or blocked stops before any model call. The Architect then proposes a typed plan from assured graph evidence and curated Wiki guidance, the Engineer generates approved files and tests, and the Validator critiques immutable receipts. The workflow uses bounded ReAct-inspired Perceive–Plan–Act–Reflect reasoning with typed artifacts and durable checkpoints.
Answer5: The project evolved from a broad automation concept into a bounded, auditable capstone prototype. Generic retrieval was refined into a curated, versioned LLM Wiki with deterministic exact/metadata retrieval and optional semantic support. Tree of Thought was evaluated and rejected because parallel speculative branches would complicate scope authority, evidence lineage, latency, and approval. The final design uses one sequential candidate with at most one evidence-directed correction. Validation also moved away from comparing generated code with stored “golden” outputs: the model now generates its own code and tests, while independent controller-owned contracts and behavior tests assess arbitrary implementations.
Answer6: The implementation uses Python, LangGraph, strict Pydantic contracts and JSON Schemas, SHA-256-bound artifacts, and durable local checkpoints. Salesforce and MuleSoft analyzers build revision-bound dependency graphs; a deterministic independent reconciliation pass produces GraphAssuranceReport before Wiki or model access. Its digest and status are bound into planning, manifests, run evidence, replay, human decisions, and final review. The authenticated Claude CLI adapter uses strict structured output with native tools disabled. The browser supports conversation, scenario selection, approvals, progress, validation evidence, diffs, and export. Candidates run only in isolated workspaces. Salesforce uses structural/security checks, candidate Jest tests, and controller LWC tests; Mule uses static contracts and an attested Maven/MUnit boundary.
Answer7: The final 2026-08-30 quality gate passed 2,111 automated tests in 604.41 seconds, plus Ruff format/lint, mypy over 70 source files, the 60-package lock check, schema/registry, and source/wheel build. Claude Account/Contact completed attempt one with 7/7 checks, 9/9 candidate Jest tests, and 10/10 controller tests. Case completed both a bounded recovery run and a clean attempt-one run; BW approved the latter candidate, diff, and evidence. Mule produced six files and passed three static checks, while MUnit/runtime checks were unavailable. BW reviewed all 18 corrected benchmark cells: all were accepted and semantically conformant, with 390/390 dependency recall, zero high-impact misses, zero authorization violations, and zero escaped defects. Expected-outcome conformance was 13/18; unavailable Wiki attribution and Mule runtime evidence keep the quality gate false.
Answer8: Authority is separated from model reasoning. Controller-owned launch contracts fix the scenario, revision, versions, paths, checks, and output inventory. A model cannot declare a graph complete: only deterministic GraphAssuranceReport logic can return assured. Non-assured evidence creates a digest-bound PlanningIntervention before model access. Source and evidence are SHA-256 bound, writes occur in isolated workspaces, and change sets come from disk bytes. Strict schemas, path policies, secret scanning, redaction, allowlisted shell-free commands, replay protection, and fail-closed dispositions address unsafe output. A late dependency omission or incorrect edge is PLAN_INVALID and requires graph regeneration, a new manifest digest, and new human approval, never Engineer attempt two. Agents cannot deploy, publish, commit, or modify legacy inputs.
Answer9: Evidence covers three bounded synthetic scenarios, not arbitrary repositories or production use. Graph assurance is bounded reconciliation, not proof that dynamic, reflective, unsupported, or external dependencies are discoverable; those require review or a safe stop. Reviewer attestations are content-bound, not authenticated. BW approved the final Case candidate; Salesforce org compilation is unclaimed. Mule lacks an attested runtime, so MUnit behavior remains unverified. The fully reviewed 18-cell historical benchmark quality gate is false: expected outcome was 13/18, and Wiki attribution and Mule runtime evidence were unavailable. It predates GraphAssuranceReport, so it makes no Wiki-benefit or assurance-runtime claim. Next: record the demo and submit.
